coherence.reasons: Both lead with the same governing thought and support it with correctly computed unit economics, runway and the software alternative. X's hierarchy is tighter: its four executive-summary pillars (market, economics, funding, alternative) map one-to-one onto the six-condition hypothesis table on slide 3 and onto the slide sections, so each slide title is a sub-claim of a pillar. Y is compact and mostly consistent, but its market slide has no place in the executive summary. Y's slide 6 title ('at best break even') also sits awkwardly with its own figure of −$1.76 for best-observed inputs, reaching near break-even only by adding a 2% promotion rate that no site has shown. X has its own blemish: the slide 7 sensitivity chart values appear rotated against their labels (riders shown as +0.22 where the title and arithmetic imply −0.31), so the chart contradicts its title. On balance X's structure is slightly more consistent.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (do not launch, back software, sell fast delivery to grocers) and both set re-entry triggers observed through customer sites. X weighs the alternatives more fully. It explicitly builds and rejects a one-store pilot (loses money at median, breaches runway in month 10, little new learning), which pre-empts the 'launch one city to prove density' fallback, and it also rejects extending the pop-up. It tests the software alternative against the investors' actual objective (profitability within current cash) and names the condition under which it fails (ARR growth below 34%). It phases hires against signed contracts and sets a 90-day checkpoint. Y's comparison is only operator versus supplier. It adds two good points: customer-conflict risk, and that the software edge is already in the 14-site benchmark. But Y never tests whether software itself meets the profitability and runway constraint, and does not address a smaller test option.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: −$6.17, −$1.76, −$12.57, +$2.02, 41.5% CAGR, $2.5M or about 6 months of runway, and −$1.05 for the median store with Zipcart's moves. Y's additional figures all check out: 3.75 orders per rider-hour to break even before store cost, +$3.97 for best-observed with Zipcart levers, $0.29–0.42 per order for each $1 of rider wage, $16.7M if the plan sits on top of core burn, and 19 orders to repay acquisition cost. Y is also disciplined about what the pack does not give, such as close rates, and treats full pipeline ARR as an upper bound. X uses more evidence, including a strong scale sanity check ($266M of plan GMV against QuickBasket's $210M revenue) and a break-even density of 1,042 orders a day under Zipcart's moves. But X has a real error: the slide 7 sensitivity values are mislabelled, with riders, density and promotions rotated. X also calls 1,042 orders a day 'top-quartile' without support. Its headline software claim (break-even in month 26, 34% growth threshold) rests on a constructed model with opex held flat while ARR nearly triples; this is disclosed as optimistic but goes beyond the pack. Y's weaker spots are milder: the 'at best break even' title and an unclear fallback in 'survives missing any one target'. Y makes fewer errors and unsupported claims.

revision.reasons: Both correctly reject the founders' hypothesis and both engage with the evidence that partly supports it. Each gives a fair caveat on the six-week pop-up and treats Zipcart's densest-city result as real but conditional on a fee, a promotion cut and a volume loss. X handles the hypothesis more explicitly: slide 3 states it, breaks it into six conditions that would have to be true, tests each, and then says what would change its mind. It also converts the Zipcart evidence into a concrete break-even density (about 1,042 orders a day) that feeds its triggers. Y's strength is showing that best-observed inputs with Zipcart's levers would be positive (+$3.97), and rebutting the founders' capability claim by noting the benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software. Both are appropriate; X's treatment is somewhat more systematic.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision on sound, correctly computed unit economics and runway, and both avoid every trap in the key. Y is cleaner and more economical, with fewer numerical blemishes and some sharp points (software edge already in the benchmark, customer conflict, rider-wage sensitivity). X serves the decision better on what the board will actually argue about. It answers the investors' question of whether the alternative reaches profitability within current cash, with a stated growth threshold. It closes off the likely founder fallback of a single-city pilot. It gives sequenced decisions with a checkpoint. Its chart mislabelling and model-heavy software projection reduce the margin, but do not change the conclusions.
